Twelve Tribes
twĕlv trībz
n. phrase (the descendants of Jacob's twelve sons, constituted as the nation Israel; and the number's use for the whole people of God)
Hebrew shebet, a rod or sceptre and so a tribe — the clan under one staff. The twelve are counted differently in different lists: Levi is set apart and Joseph divided into Ephraim and Manasseh, so the number is kept while the names shift.

Biblical Definition

The twelve tribes are constituted at Jacob's deathbed: “All these are the twelve tribes of Israel: and this is it that their father spake unto them, and blessed them” (Gen 49:28). They are carried on the high priest's heart: twelve stones on the breastplate, “according to the twelve tribes” (Exo 28:21). James writes to them as the scattered church: “to the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad, greeting” (Jas 1:1). The Lord assigns them judges: “ye also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Mat 19:28). And their names are on the gates of the city: “twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and names written thereon, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel” (Rev 21:12).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines tribe as a family, race or series of generations, descending from the same progenitor and kept distinct, as in the case of the twelve tribes of Israel, descended from the sons of Jacob.

expand to see more

TRIBE, n. A family, race or series of generations, descending from the same progenitor, and kept distinct, as in the case of the twelve tribes of Israel, descended from the sons of Jacob.

2. A division, class or distinct portion of people, from whatever cause that distinction may have originated.

3. A number of things having certain characters or resemblances in common.

Key Scripture

Gen 49:28 — "All these are the twelve tribes of Israel: and this is it that their father spake unto them, and blessed them; every one according to his blessing he blessed them."

Exo 28:21 — "And the stones shall be with the names of the children of Israel, twelve, according to their names, like the engravings of a signet; every one with his name shall they be according to the twelve tribes."

Jas 1:1 — "James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad, greeting."

Mat 19:28 — "And Jesus said unto them, Verily I say unto you, That ye which have followed me, in the regeneration when the Son of man shall sit in the throne of his glory, ye also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel."

Rev 21:12 — "And had a wall great and high, and had twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and names written thereon, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel:"

Modern Corruption

The tribes are treated as a closed ethnic register, and James addresses the church by their name in the first verse of his letter.

expand to see more

James 1:1 is the verse that governs how the New Testament uses the number. He writes to the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad, and the letter that follows is plainly to Christians — brethren who hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, who meet in an assembly, who are warned about their tongues. Either James is writing only to converted Jews of the dispersion, or he is using Israel's oldest self-description for the whole people of God. Peter does the same with the terms of Exodus 19 in 1 Peter 2:9. The Reformed have read both as the second, without denying the first was also literally true of many of the readers.

That reading is not a spiritualising trick; it is what the lists themselves do. Levi is omitted from the land-tribes and Joseph is split so that the count stays at twelve; Dan is missing from Revelation 7 and Joseph appears alongside Manasseh. The number is held constant while the membership is adjusted, which means twelve was always a statement about wholeness rather than a census. Revelation 21 sets the twelve tribes on the gates and the twelve apostles on the foundations of one city, and the church has taken that as its own architecture ever since.

Exodus 28 supplies the tenderest use and it belongs in any pastor's thinking about his people. Aaron carried the twelve names on his breastplate over his heart when he went in before the LORD, and on two onyx stones on his shoulders — the whole nation, borne into the presence of God by one man, by name. Hebrews says the true High Priest ever liveth to make intercession; He carries the names too, and none of the lists in Scripture is as long as His.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shebet (H7626) and matteh (H4294), tribe — both also mean a rod or staff; shneim asar (H8147, H6240), twelve; Greek dodekaphulon (G1429), the twelve tribes.

expand to see more

Hebrew shibte Yisrael (H7626) — the tribes of Israel; Genesis 49:28, Exodus 28:21, Deuteronomy 33:5, 1 Kings 11:31.

Greek dodeka phulai (G1427, G5443) — twelve tribes; Matthew 19:28, James 1:1, Revelation 21:12; dodekaphulon, Acts 26:7 only.

Greek diaspora (G1290) — the scattering, dispersion; James 1:1, 1 Peter 1:1, John 7:35.

Usage

"“To the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad” — and the letter is to the church."

"“According to the twelve tribes” — carried on the high priest's heart, by name."

"“Names written thereon” — on the gates, with the apostles on the foundations."
